tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: small — keep workflows under 5 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A proposal the user already started, dismissed or let expire is reported back (a dismissed or expired proposal's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__start_session
tools.description:
Start a separate Claude Code session for a task while you stay with the user (when: see "Starting other sessions"). `initiation` says who wants it: "user_asked" starts it now and returns its id; "offer" is for a task the user named in their latest message (new work here, or "suggest / split off / make a task or session for X"): called with a title alone, it shows a "New session" / "Do it here" card and WAITS for their answer, so it must be the only call in that message (no update_plan, no other tool); the result then tells you to carry on here, or to send the brief with proposal_id so the session starts; "own_initiative" is for work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up (when your reply calls work a follow-up or a separate PR, propose it here rather than only saying so); the user sees a card and nothing runs until they start it, by clicking it or by telling you (then call this again with just proposal_id).
"user_asked" and "own_initiative" both need a `prompt` — the brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like — and the call is refused without it; `background` does not stand in for it. Only an "offer" is a title alone.
context: "fork" = this whole conversation + your `prompt`. "fresh" (default) = your `prompt` + `background` only, so `background` is required too, at least 80 characters.
Checkout here ("fresh" only): use_worktree false = shares this checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session its branch and PR too: never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); true = its own worktree (the default when this session is in one).
Elsewhere ("fresh", user_asked only, when the user named the place): `cwd`, `target` "ssh" + `host`, `environment` or `preset`; list_start_targets lists the valid names.
Right before calling, write its bold title line and one sentence on what it will do; it has started only once this returns saying so. Never wait for it or poll.

context: "fork" = this whole conversation + your `prompt`. "fresh" (default) = your `prompt` + `background` only, so `background` is required too, at least 80 characters.

initiation.description: "user_asked": the user asked in words for separate, parallel or background work, or told you to start this piece — it starts now. "offer": a task the user named in their latest message (new work for this session, or one they asked you to suggest, split off or make a session for) — the user is asked first and the call waits for their answer; send only title with it (the brief follows, with proposal_id, if they choose New session). "own_initiative": work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up; it waits as a proposal card until the user starts it; never for a task the user's message tells you to do. Required unless proposal_id is set.

proposal_id.description: Start a proposal the user told you to start, exactly as proposed: its task_id and nothing else (wake_when_done may accompany a local one). To change it, dismiss_task it and start a new session.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task. Shown on the row or card. Required unless proposal_id is set.

prompt.description: The brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like. Required for "user_asked" and "own_initiative" — the call is refused without it, and `background` does not stand in for it; an "offer" leaves it out (the card shows the user's own message) and you send it with proposal_id once they choose New session.

context.description: "fresh" (default) or "fork" — see the tool description. A "fork" from a worktree session gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip (commit first; uncommitted edits stay here); from a plain checkout it shares the folder.

background.description: Required with "fresh", besides `prompt`: at least 80 characters of overall goal, decisions and constraints so far, how this piece fits — for someone who has not seen this conversation. Ignored for "fork".

wake_when_done.description: Once this session (and any sibling still working) ends its turn, or fails to start (unless it waits at a prompt the user answers there, its folder was never opened in Claude Desktop, or the user started, stopped or archived it), and you are idle, the app continues you, whether or not this is set. true also continues you if this session never gets its task some other way, such as a brief that is not sent; default false; not with own_initiative; ignored with target "cloud", which never continues you.

name.description: Optional short handle for the session ([a-z0-9-], ≤24), e.g. "cli-cleanup". Linked sessions and plan steps refer to it by this name; derived from the title when omitted.

use_worktree.description: "fresh" only (rejected with "fork"). false = shares this session's checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session: its worktree, branch and PR, so never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); not accepted from a session set up to move from the user's checkout into a worktree with EnterWorktree (before or after it moves), one working in a worktree on an SSH host, or one whose worktree was given back. At another place named by `cwd`, `host` or `preset`, false = that folder as it is. true = its own git worktree. Omitted: the same folder when this session works in a plain folder and has never had a worktree (its own, a shared one, or one it will enter later); otherwise its own worktree. Omitted with `preset` or `host`, or with `cwd` from a session on an SSH host: the default set on that preset or SSH connection instead.

model.description: "fresh" only, optional: a cheaper model id for mechanical or read-only pieces (e.g. a Sonnet or Haiku id). Same family or cheaper than yours; anything higher is ignored. Omit to inherit yours.

target.description: "fresh" only. "local" (default) = where this session runs. "cloud" = run it as a cloud session (keeps going when this computer sleeps). Needs the repository on GitHub and a cloud environment — the app checks and tells the user if it cannot, and the task then stays as a card for them to start. It starts from this session's pushed branch when it runs in a worktree, else the repository's default branch. model/effort/use_worktree/cwd/source_branch do not apply. Only when the user asks for the cloud. "ssh" = on the SSH connection named by host (or by a preset).

host.description: With target "ssh": the name of one of the user's saved SSH connections (as list_start_targets reports it) — never a raw hostname, user or key. The app connects as the user configured it and may ask them to sign in.

cwd.description: The folder the session works in, when it is not this project: an absolute (or ~/) path on the host it will run on — this computer, this session's host, or the SSH connection named by host (default there: the connection's folder). Must exist; if the user has not trusted it yet the app asks them first. "fresh" only.

environment.description: With target "cloud": the name or id of one of the user's cloud environments (list_start_targets lists them); omitted = the default one. Self-hosted environments and runner pools need the user's own click and are refused, and so is an environment that cannot run this project's repository.

source_branch.description: The existing local branch the new worktree is cut from. Default in this project: this session's base branch (the one picked when it started, or the one its worktree was cut from). If the session has none and either it runs on an SSH host or its project folder is itself a git worktree or submodule, the folder's current commit. Otherwise, the repository's default branch, or the folder's current commit if that is unknown. Only for a session that gets its own worktree (use_worktree true, or the place's default); not with target "cloud".

branch_name.description: A short slug for the new worktree's branch (the app adds the user's branch prefix and a suffix). Only with a worktree.

preset.description: The name of one of the user's saved session presets on this computer: it names the place itself (a folder here or an SSH connection and folder — do not pass host or cwd with it) and brings model, effort and worktree defaults plus its saved environment variables; use_worktree/model/effort override those. Cloud and Remote Control presets are not available here.

effort.description: "fresh" only, optional: reasoning effort at or below yours. Omit to inherit.

permission_mode.description: Optional, local starts only: the permission mode it starts in — this session's own or a lower one (omit to inherit it). A higher mode, or one the app does not offer here, is refused; raising a session is set_session_permission_mode's card to show.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work: the user follows your progress by it and will never ask for it, so it is part of the task. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: propose it and call this.

The result says which case below applies. When the box shows your question, it ends your turn: write no text after this call, since the recap and question say what the user needs and your work above holds the detail. Otherwise your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, with any question the box did not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. entries.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using `find`/Glob, `grep`/Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

entries.name: ExitPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

<system-reminder>
Plan mode is active. The user indicated that they do not want you to execute yet -- you MUST NOT make any edits (with the exception of the plan file mentioned below), run any non-readonly tools (including changing configs or making commits), or otherwise make any changes to the system. This supercedes any other instructions you have received.

## Plan File Info:
No plan file exists yet. You should create your plan at /Users/jens/.claude/plans/virtual-singing-bengio.md using the Write tool.
You should build your plan incrementally by writing to or editing this file. NOTE that this is the only file you are allowed to edit - other than this you are only allowed to take READ-ONLY actions.

## Plan Workflow

### Phase 1: Initial Understanding
Goal: Gain a comprehensive understanding of the user's request by reading through code and asking them questions. Critical: In this phase you should only use the Explore subagent type.

1. Focus on understanding the user's request and the code associated with their request. Actively search for existing functions, utilities, and patterns that can be reused — avoid proposing new code when suitable implementations already exist.

2. **Launch up to 3 Explore agents IN PARALLEL** (single message, multiple tool calls) to efficiently explore the codebase.
   - Use 1 agent when the task is isolated to known files, the user provided specific file paths, or you're making a small targeted change.
   - Use multiple agents when: the scope is uncertain, multiple areas of the codebase are involved, or you need to understand existing patterns before planning.
   - Quality over quantity - 3 agents maximum, but you should try to use the minimum number of agents necessary (usually just 1)
   - If using multiple agents: Provide each agent with a specific search focus or area to explore. Example: One agent searches for existing implementations, another explores related components, a third investigating testing patterns

### Phase 2: Design
Goal: Design an implementation approach.

Launch Plan agent(s) to design the implementation based on the user's intent and your exploration results from Phase 1.

You can launch up to 1 agent(s) in parallel.

**Guidelines:**
- **Default**: Launch at least 1 Plan agent for most tasks - it helps validate your understanding and consider alternatives
- **Skip agents**: Only for truly trivial tasks (typo fixes, single-line changes, simple renames)

In the agent prompt:
- Provide comprehensive background context from Phase 1 exploration including filenames and code path traces
- Describe requirements and constraints
- Request a detailed implementation plan

### Phase 3: Review
Goal: Review the plan(s) from Phase 2 and ensure alignment with the user's intentions.
1. Read the critical files you identified during exploration to deepen your understanding
2. Ensure that the plans align with the user's original request
3. Use AskUserQuestion to clarify any remaining questions with the user

### Phase 4: Final Plan
Goal: Write your final plan to the plan file (the only file you can edit).
- Begin with a **Context** section: explain why this change is being made — the problem or need it addresses, what prompted it, and the intended outcome
- Include only your recommended approach, not all alternatives
- Ensure that the plan file is concise enough to scan quickly, but detailed enough to execute effectively
- Name the critical files to be modified. For changes that repeat a pattern across many files, describe the pattern once and list a few representative paths — do not enumerate every file or line number
- Reference existing functions and utilities you found that should be reused, with their file paths
- Include a verification section describing how to test the changes end-to-end (run the code, use MCP tools, run tests)

### Phase 5: Call ExitPlanMode
At the very end of your turn, once you have asked the user questions and are happy with your final plan file - you should always call ExitPlanMode to indicate to the user that you are done planning.
This is critical - your turn should only end with either using the AskUserQuestion tool OR calling ExitPlanMode. Do not stop unless it's for these 2 reasons

**Important:** Use AskUserQuestion ONLY to clarify requirements or choose between approaches. Use ExitPlanMode to request plan approval. Do NOT ask about plan approval in any other way - no text questions, no AskUserQuestion. Phrases like "Is this plan okay?", "Should I proceed?", "How does this plan look?", "Any changes before we start?", or similar MUST use ExitPlanMode.

NOTE: At any point in time through this workflow you should feel free to ask the user questions or clarifications using the AskUserQuestion tool. Don't make large assumptions about user intent. The goal is to present a well researched plan to the user, and tie any loose ends before implementation begins.
</system-reminder>

vars:

  PROJECT:

    vars:

      - echo "📦 Syncing dependencies..."

      - uv tool list | grep -q pre-commit || uv tool install pre-commit
      - git rev-parse --git-dir >/dev/null 2>&1 || git init -b main
      - uv run pre-commit install
      - uv run alembic upgrade head

    desc: Install dependencies using uv

  init:
    desc: Initialize project (install python, sync deps, setup pre-commit)
    vars:
      PYTHON_VERSION:
        sh: |
          grep 'requires-python' pyproject.toml | sed -E 's/.*>=?([0-9]+\.[0-9]+).*/\1/'
    cmds:
      - echo "🐍 Installing Python {{.PYTHON_VERSION}}..."
      - uv python install {{.PYTHON_VERSION}}
      - uv python pin {{.PYTHON_VERSION}}
      - echo "📦 Syncing dependencies..."
      - uv sync
      - echo "🔒 Installing pre-commit hooks..."
      - uv tool list | grep -q pre-commit || uv tool install pre-commit
      - git rev-parse --git-dir >/dev/null 2>&1 || git init -b main
      - uv run pre-commit install
      - uv run alembic upgrade head

  sync:
    desc: Install dependencies using uv

# alloq als Desktop-App

Die Desktop-App ist eine Tauri-App mit eingebettetem Python-Backend
(reflex-desktop). Sie nutzt die zentrale Postgres-Datenbank und enthält keine
Geheimnisse: Jede Person meldet sich mit Microsoft Entra ID an und verbindet
sich mit ihrem eigenen Zugriffstoken mit Postgres.

## Ablauf der Anmeldung

1. „Mit Microsoft anmelden“ nutzt zuerst das gespeicherte Konto aus dem
   macOS-Schlüsselbund (Eintrag `alloq` / `entra-token-cache`). Gibt es keins,
   öffnet MSAL die Anmeldung im Standardbrowser (Authorization Code Flow mit
   PKCE, Rückleitung auf `http://localhost`).
2. Jede neue Datenbankverbindung bekommt Benutzer und Token der angemeldeten
   Person (`app/desktop/entra.py`). Vor der Anmeldung gibt es keine
   Verbindung.
3. Die App prüft die Schema-Version (`alembic_version`) gegen
   `app/desktop/schema.py`. Passt sie nicht, bricht die Anmeldung mit einem
   Hinweis ab. Migrationen laufen nur auf dem Server.
4. Die App sucht den alloq-Benutzer mit derselben E-Mail-Adresse (Groß- und
   Kleinschreibung egal) und öffnet die normale appkit-Sitzung. Neue Benutzer
   legt die Desktop-App nicht an.

Nach einem Neustart stellt die App das Microsoft-Konto aus dem Schlüsselbund
still wieder her, sobald sie die Datenbank braucht. Ist die alloq-Sitzung noch
gültig, geht es ohne Anmeldeseite weiter. Das Zugriffstoken erneuert ein
Hintergrund-Thread kurz vor Ablauf.

„Abmelden“ beendet die Sitzung, vergisst das Microsoft-Konto auf diesem Mac und
schließt alle Datenbankverbindungen.
---
# Umsetzungsplan: Übersicht als Portfolio (Variante C)

Grundlage ist der Entwurf C „Portfolio“ im Design-Artefakt
https://claude.ai/artifact/7YFv9dz5VcSEzN4nqaioax. Die Übersicht (`/`) zeigt danach vier
Karten: Zeit und Fortschritt je Projekt, offene Risiken als Matrix, den kritischen
Ressourcenpfad und die Kapazität je Rolle. Oben in der Werkzeugleiste wählt man den
Bereich: ganze Abteilung oder direkt unterstellt.

## Ziel

Die Abteilungsleitung sieht auf einen Blick, wie die Projekte stehen, ob die Kapazität
reicht, welche Risiken drücken und an welcher Rolle oder Person das Enddatum hängt.
Jede Zahl kommt aus vorhandenen Daten. Es gibt keine neuen Tabellen und keine Migration.

## Begriffe und Regeln

# alloq als Desktop-App

Die Desktop-App ist eine Tauri-App mit eingebettetem Python-Backend
(reflex-desktop). Sie nutzt die zentrale Postgres-Datenbank und enthält keine
Geheimnisse: Jede Person meldet sich mit Microsoft Entra ID an und verbindet
sich mit ihrem eigenen Zugriffstoken mit Postgres.

## Ablauf der Anmeldung

1. „Mit Microsoft anmelden“ nutzt zuerst das gespeicherte Konto aus dem
   macOS-Schlüsselbund (Eintrag `alloq` / `entra-token-cache`). Gibt es keins,
   öffnet MSAL die Anmeldung im Standardbrowser (Authorization Code Flow mit
   PKCE, Rückleitung auf `http://localhost`).
2. Jede neue Datenbankverbindung bekommt Benutzer und Token der angemeldeten
   Person (`app/desktop/entra.py`). Vor der Anmeldung gibt es keine
   Verbindung.
3. Die App prüft die Schema-Version (`alembic_version`) gegen
   `app/desktop/schema.py`. Passt sie nicht, bricht die Anmeldung mit einem
   Hinweis ab. Migrationen laufen nur auf dem Server.
4. Die App sucht den alloq-Benutzer mit derselben E-Mail-Adresse (Groß- und
   Kleinschreibung egal) und öffnet die normale appkit-Sitzung. Neue Benutzer
   legt die Desktop-App nicht an.

Nach einem Neustart stellt die App das Microsoft-Konto aus dem Schlüsselbund
still wieder her, sobald sie die Datenbank braucht. Ist die alloq-Sitzung noch
gültig, geht es ohne Anmeldeseite weiter. Das Zugriffstoken erneuert ein
Hintergrund-Thread kurz vor Ablauf.

„Abmelden“ beendet die Sitzung, vergisst das Microsoft-Konto auf diesem Mac und
schließt alle Datenbankverbindungen.

# Refined prompt: Alloq developer documentation workflow

> This is the boosted prompt. Approving it hands it over for execution as a
> multi-agent Workflow (medium scale, about 10 to 14 agents).

## Task

Run a multi-agent workflow that writes the Alloq developer documentation as a
VitePress site in `docs/`. The core of the docs is every implemented feature written
as a user story with acceptance criteria. The stories are grouped in a user story
map. Every story and every criterion must come from the code, with links to the
source files and tests that prove it. Write the docs one page at a time. A new
developer, or an AI agent, should be able to read the site and understand what Alloq
does, how it is built, and where each behaviour lives in the code.

## Context (found in the repo)

- **Docs tooling already planned but missing:** `taskfiles/Taskfile.docs.yml` defines
  `task docs:install|dev|build|preview` for a VitePress site in `docs/`. The folder
  does not exist yet. Create it to match these tasks (`npm run docs:dev`,
  `docs:build`, `docs:preview`).
- **Existing docs to reuse, not delete:** `README.md` (features, stack, setup),
  `doc/desktop.md` (German, desktop sign-in flow), `doc/plans/*.md` (German feature
  plans, for example the dashboard portfolio rules), `doc/architecture/alloq-architecture.html`
  and `.json` (component diagram), screenshots `doc/*.png`.
- **Architecture map:** `.claude/skills/alloq-implementation/SKILL.md` and its
  `references/architecture.md` describe the layers (Entity, Model, Repository,
  Service, State, Component, Page, Registration, Migration) and the package split.
  Use them as the starting point, then check them against the code.
- **Host app** `app/`: `app/app.py` registers all pages (login, profile, password
  reset, users, roles, departments, holidays, team overview, projects overview,
  planning at `/` and its own route, dashboard at `/dashboard`), the session guard
  and HTTPS middleware. Admin pages are in `app/pages/`, sidebar in
  `app/components/sidebar.py`, desktop-only code in `app/desktop/`.
- **Workspace packages** in `components/`:
  - `alloq-commons`: entities, models, repositories, shared services
    (`utilization.py`, `quick_project.py`), shared UI (list view, toolbar, shell,
    excel grid, dialogs), `roles.py`, `access.py`, `theme.py`, department, role and
    holiday states.
  - `alloq-project`: project list, project form and inspector (status, risk,
    resource tabs), plan modal, planning grid, Gantt view, planning filters,
    absence view, view settings, forecast, plan distribution.
  - `alloq-team`: team overview, employee table, cards, inspector and form.
  - `alloq-dashboard`: KPI cards, utilization, capacity, earned value, top risks,
    portfolio (bubbles, resource path, risks), drill-down drawers, aggregation
    services.
- **Access levels:** admin can do everything; project_manager edits planning
  (handlers guarded by `@requires_editor`) but has no administration; employee only
  reads. `tests/test_handler_authorization.py` enforces this for every handler.
- **Guard tests that describe system rules:** `tests/test_component_boundaries.py`
  (package import direction), `tests/test_handler_authorization.py`,
  `tests/test_migrations.py`, `tests/test_configuration_profiles.py`.
- **Config:** `configuration/config*.yaml` profiles (local, prod, desktop,
  desktop_fake, devcontainer, docker_test) with env `__` overrides.
- **Migrations:** 12 hand-written Alembic files in `alembic/versions/`.
- **Desktop:** Tauri shell in `tauri/` with embedded Python, Entra ID sign-in, Postgres
  access with personal tokens, schema version check in `app/desktop/schema.py`.
- **UI text is German.** Quote German labels exactly as the UI shows them, with an
  English meaning in brackets the first time.
- **Working tree:** branch `feature/planning-readability` has uncommitted changes
  (for example `services/planning_view_settings.py`). Document the working tree as it
  is when the workflow starts, and record the commit hash plus "with uncommitted
  changes" on the index page.

## Requirements

### Documentation method

1. Structure the site with **Diátaxis**: Guide (tutorial and how-to), Architecture
   (explanation, arc42-lite), Features (user stories, reference), Reference
   (data model, configuration, commands, glossary).
2. Draw architecture with **C4 levels** in Mermaid: system context, containers (web
   app, desktop app, Postgres, Entra ID), components (the four packages and the host
   app). Add one ER diagram of the entities.
3. Build the story map in the **Jeff Patton** shape: a backbone of user activities
   left to right, user tasks under each activity, stories under each task. Show it
   as a Markdown table plus one Mermaid diagram. Every story ID in the map links to
   its story.
4. Write stories in **INVEST** shape: `As a <persona>, I want <goal>, so that
   <benefit>`. Personas come from the code: Administrator, Project manager,
   Employee, Desktop user. Use one persona per story.
5. Write acceptance criteria as **Given / When / Then**. Each criterion must match a
   concrete rule in the code: a validation limit (`Field(max_length=...)`), a guard
   (`@requires_editor`), a filter, a calculation in a service, an empty state, an
   error message.

### Grounding rules (most important)

6. Each story carries an **Evidence** block: source files with the symbol names
   (state class, handler, service function, component) and the tests that cover it,
   as relative links from the page to the file.
7. A criterion with no covering test is marked `(no test)`. Never invent a feature,
   a rule or a limit. If behaviour is unclear, write it under "Open questions" on the
   story page instead of guessing.
8. Every file path and symbol named in the docs must exist. The verification phase
   checks this with `grep` or `rg`.
9. Story IDs are stable and readable: `<AREA>-<NN>`, for example `PLAN-03`, `TEAM-01`,
   `DASH-05`, `ADM-02`, `AUTH-01`, `DESK-01`.

### Pages (write one page per writer step)

10. `docs/index.md`: what Alloq is, who uses it, how to read the docs, the commit
    the docs were verified against.
11. `docs/guide/getting-started.md`: prerequisites, `task init`, `task sync`, run the
    app, config profiles, test login hint without credentials, `task test/lint/format/typecheck`.
12. `docs/guide/contributing.md`: the workflow from the alloq-implementation skill
    (where code goes, tests first, gates, file size limit, hand-written migrations),
    told for a new developer.
13. `docs/architecture/overview.md`: C4 context and container diagrams, package
    split and dependency direction, request flow from a page to the database.
14. `docs/architecture/layers.md`: each layer with the departments slice as the
    worked example, real file paths.
15. `docs/architecture/data-model.md`: ER diagram and one table per entity (fields,
    relations, constraints), taken from `alloq_commons/entities/`.
16. `docs/architecture/security-and-access.md`: session guard, roles, `access.py`,
    `@requires_editor`, the authorization test, OAuth and password reset.
17. `docs/architecture/desktop.md`: English version of `doc/desktop.md`, checked
    against `app/desktop/` and `tauri/`.
18. `docs/architecture/calculations.md`: how utilization, capacity, forecast, plan
    distribution, earned value and the portfolio buffer are calculated, with the
    service functions that do it.
19. `docs/features/story-map.md`: the story map.
20. `docs/features/<area>.md`, one page per backbone activity, holding its stories.
    Expected areas (confirm in the inventory phase): sign in and access;
    administration (users, roles, departments, public holidays); team and
    employees with absences; projects (list, form, status, risks, required
    capacity, plan); capacity planning (grid, Gantt, filters, view settings,
    absence view); dashboard and portfolio; desktop app.
21. `docs/reference/configuration.md`, `docs/reference/commands.md` (all `task`
    targets from `Taskfile.dist.yml` and `taskfiles/`), `docs/reference/testing.md`
    (test layout, guard tests, how to write state tests), `docs/reference/glossary.md`
    (German UI term, English term, meaning).
22. Each page starts with YAML frontmatter: `title`, `description`, `story_ids` (on
    feature pages), `source_paths`, `last_verified_commit`. This helps AI agents load
    the right page.
23. Add `docs/llms.txt`: a short plain list of all pages with one line each, so an AI
    agent can find its way in.

### VitePress site

24. Add `docs/package.json` with scripts `docs:dev`, `docs:build`, `docs:preview`,
    `vitepress` and `vitepress-plugin-mermaid` with exact pinned versions (look up
    current stable versions with Context7 before pinning).
25. Add `docs/.vitepress/config.mts` with nav and sidebar for the four sections,
    local search, and the Mermaid plugin.
26. Add `docs/node_modules`, `docs/.vitepress/dist` and `docs/.vitepress/cache` to
    `.gitignore`.
27. Add a short "Documentation" section to `README.md` that links to `docs/` and
    names `task docs:install` and `task docs:dev`.

### Writing style

28. Use the `plain-writing` skill for all prose: simple words, complete sentences,
    no filler. Keep each page under about 400 lines; split a feature area into two
    pages when it grows past that.

## Workflow design (medium, about 12 agents)

Load the `workflow-authoring` skill before writing the script. Phases:

1. **Inventory** (1 agent): list routes and page factories, every state class with
   its `@rx.event` handlers and guards, entities, repositories, services and test
   files. Output a JSON inventory grouped by proposed area.
2. **Scan** (5 agents in parallel, one per area group: project and planning; team;
   dashboard; commons and admin pages; auth, access and desktop): read the code and
   tests for the area and return draft stories as JSON (id, persona, story, criteria,
   evidence paths and symbols, tests, open questions).
3. **Map** (1 agent): merge the drafts, remove duplicates, fix IDs, build the backbone
   and the story map.
4. **Write** (about 4 agents, pipelined page by page): guide pages, architecture
   pages, feature pages, reference pages. Each writer gets the inventory, the story
   JSON and the page list.
5. **Verify** (2 agents, adversarial): one checks every path, symbol and criterion
   against the code and the tests; one checks the site builds
   (`task docs:install && task docs:build`), links resolve, and every story ID in the
   map has a story. Return a list of defects.
6. **Fix**: the main session fixes the reported defects and builds again.

## Deliverables

- `docs/` VitePress site with the pages listed in requirements 10 to 23.
- `docs/package.json`, `docs/.vitepress/config.mts`, `docs/llms.txt`.
- `.gitignore` and `README.md` updates.
- No changes to application code, tests or migrations.

## Success criteria

- `task docs:install && task docs:build` finishes without errors or dead-link
  warnings.
- Every story has a persona, at least two Given/When/Then criteria, and an Evidence
  block whose paths and symbols exist (checked with `rg`).
- Every page, route and guarded handler in the inventory is covered by at least one
  story, or listed on the story map page under "Not covered" with a reason.
- The story map links every story ID, and every feature page links back to the map.
- A spot check of five random criteria against the code finds no invented rule.
- `task docs:dev` shows the site with working nav, sidebar, search and Mermaid
  diagrams (check it in the browser pane).

## Out of scope

- Changing application code, tests, migrations or configuration.
- Features that exist only in `doc/plans/` and are not in the code.
- End-user help in German, API reference generated from docstrings, deployment of
  the docs site.
- Deleting or rewriting the existing `doc/` folder.
- Committing; leave the changes in the working tree for review.

Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

# Story Mapping: Summary of the Article

The article presents story mapping as a way to arrange a product backlog as a visual map that starts from the user's experience. It is not a formal modeling method.

## Structure

- **User tasks** are the starting point. They describe what a user wants to accomplish with the system and are arranged left to right in a sequence that tells a coherent story.
- **Activities** group related user tasks when there are many of them side by side.
- **Subtasks** sit below user tasks and describe the individual steps. They can also capture variants of how a task is carried out.
- **Stories** are the detailed items. In release-level maps, only epics and themes appear. Higher-priority items in sprint-level maps can be user stories.
- **Walking skeleton:** A rudimentary version of the product that serves as a starting base, which the article compares to a first minimum viable product.
- **Slices (releases or sprints):** Horizontal layers, often marked with masking tape, that show what is included in a given release or sprint.

## Axes

- **Horizontal:** The user's workflow, in a plausible sequence. The article notes that users sometimes take steps in a different order or skip some entirely.
- **Vertical:** Priority, meaning how important each step is for the system to support. The article says the map shows priority in this direction, and that items within a slice should be prioritized.

## Worked Example

The article uses a mobile time-tracking app. A user sets the date, start and end times, an activity, and optionally a comment, then submits the entry and later reviews or corrects it. Because most users enter times without comments, typing the time and activity matters more than the comment. Being able to record time at all matters more than the comfort of entering it.

## Release and Sprint Planning

- **Fixed-date releases:** A slice represents the currently targeted scope. Priority within the slice ensures the most valuable changes ship first.
- **Feature-based releases:** Ship small, meaningful increments as early as possible to get feedback sooner. Defer comfort features. The article summarizes this as "so klein wie möglich, so groß wie nötig" (as small as possible, as large as necessary).
- **Sprints:** Each slice can represent one sprint, with additional slices giving a look ahead.

## Personas

The article does not mention personas.

## Step-by-Step Build Process

The article does not give a formal procedure. It recommends creating the initial map in workshops with stakeholders such as users and funders, together with the development team.

## Naming Conventions

The article does not give rules for naming, such as verb-based labels.

## Best Practices

- Build the map collaboratively with stakeholders and team members, using Post-its.
- Keep the map visible in the team's workspace so it stays up to date and is easy to discuss.
- Use the map to discuss scope, estimate the whole system, and plan releases.
- Start release planning from the outcome the product should deliver, and select the part of the map needed for it.
- Use abstraction levels that match the purpose. Broad maps for multi-release planning, more detailed maps for sprint planning.
- Reflect on the map at every Scrum event: refinement, sprint planning, and review.

## Pitfalls

- Treating the map as the product owner's private document. The article argues it belongs to everyone involved.
- Using the same level of detail for multi-release planning and sprint planning.
- Expecting strict sequence. Real user behavior varies.

content.content:
# User Story Mapping: Summary of the Article

The article describes user story mapping as a technique for visualizing product requirements so that all stakeholders, including those without methodological background, share one understanding of the product and its functions. It is presented as a tool for agile transformation, though the author says it also fits classic process models.

## Purpose and Goals
- Start by agreeing on the product vision and goals, asking what customer benefit the product delivers and what problem it solves.
- Use it for medium- to long-term agile planning, project status visibility, process map development, and requirements engineering across organizational units.

## Structure
- **Activities (backbone):** The top level describes what users do with the product, written from the user's perspective and arranged left to right in chronological order.
- **Tasks:** Placed beneath each activity, summarizing the concrete steps users take. Activities and tasks together form the "backbone."
- **Stories:** Attached below the tasks on sticky notes and ordered vertically by priority, following the product backlog if one exists.
- **User story format:** Each story names a role, a functionality, and a benefit, with acceptance criteria written in informal language.

## Axes
- **Horizontal:** Chronological flow of activities and tasks.
- **Vertical:** Priority of user stories.

## Releases and Slices
- Teams draw a horizontal line separating stories needed in the near term from those that are not.
- Additional lines can mark further releases or increments, producing a prioritized sequence for delivery.
- The article does not describe a walking skeleton or personas, and it does not explicitly define an MVP. The first release line is the closest equivalent.

## Step-by-Step Method
1. Clarify the product vision, goals, and customer problem.
2. Identify activities and tasks from the user's perspective and place them on the wall in order.
3. Write user stories and attach them under the tasks.
4. Prioritize stories vertically, using the backlog if available.
5. Review as a team to merge, split, remove, or add stories, resolving inconsistencies, redundancies, and gaps.
6. Draw release or increment lines to define the delivery sequence.
7. Digitize the map by photographing it or recreating it in a diagramming tool.
8. Store it in a version-controlled documentation tool and notify stakeholders of changes.
9. Keep the map updated as changes occur.

## Naming Conventions
- Activities and tasks are described from the user's point of view. The article does not prescribe verb usage or other naming rules.
- User stories follow the role-functionality-benefit template.

## Best Practices
- Run workshops with about 4 to 8 participants.
- Agree on meeting rules to keep sessions efficient.
- For distributed teams, hold remote workshops using video conferencing and collaboration tools such as Miro, Asana, or Jira.
- Keep documentation transparent and accessible to all stakeholders.
- Treat the map as a living artifact with regular updates.

## Pitfalls
- A map created once and never updated loses its value.
- Overlapping, missing, or conflicting stories should be caught during team review.
- The article offers little further detail on common pitfalls.

## Templates and Layout
- Physical setup uses sticky notes: activities at the top, tasks beneath, stories below those, with horizontal lines for releases.
- Digital setups can use diagramming tools such as MS Visio, or collaboration boards for remote work.
- Store the final map in a versioned tool such as SharePoint or Confluence, with automatic change notifications.

# User Story Mapping: Summary of the Article

The article describes user story mapping as a technique for visualizing product requirements so that all stakeholders, including those without methodological background, share one understanding of the product and its functions. It is presented as a tool for agile transformation, though the author says it also fits classic process models.

## Purpose and Goals
- Start by agreeing on the product vision and goals, asking what customer benefit the product delivers and what problem it solves.
- Use it for medium- to long-term agile planning, project status visibility, process map development, and requirements engineering across organizational units.

## Structure
- **Activities (backbone):** The top level describes what users do with the product, written from the user's perspective and arranged left to right in chronological order.
- **Tasks:** Placed beneath each activity, summarizing the concrete steps users take. Activities and tasks together form the "backbone."
- **Stories:** Attached below the tasks on sticky notes and ordered vertically by priority, following the product backlog if one exists.
- **User story format:** Each story names a role, a functionality, and a benefit, with acceptance criteria written in informal language.

## Axes
- **Horizontal:** Chronological flow of activities and tasks.
- **Vertical:** Priority of user stories.

## Releases and Slices
- Teams draw a horizontal line separating stories needed in the near term from those that are not.
- Additional lines can mark further releases or increments, producing a prioritized sequence for delivery.
- The article does not describe a walking skeleton or personas, and it does not explicitly define an MVP. The first release line is the closest equivalent.

## Step-by-Step Method
1. Clarify the product vision, goals, and customer problem.
2. Identify activities and tasks from the user's perspective and place them on the wall in order.
3. Write user stories and attach them under the tasks.
4. Prioritize stories vertically, using the backlog if available.
5. Review as a team to merge, split, remove, or add stories, resolving inconsistencies, redundancies, and gaps.
6. Draw release or increment lines to define the delivery sequence.
7. Digitize the map by photographing it or recreating it in a diagramming tool.
8. Store it in a version-controlled documentation tool and notify stakeholders of changes.
9. Keep the map updated as changes occur.

## Naming Conventions
- Activities and tasks are described from the user's point of view. The article does not prescribe verb usage or other naming rules.
- User stories follow the role-functionality-benefit template.

## Best Practices
- Run workshops with about 4 to 8 participants.
- Agree on meeting rules to keep sessions efficient.
- For distributed teams, hold remote workshops using video conferencing and collaboration tools such as Miro, Asana, or Jira.
- Keep documentation transparent and accessible to all stakeholders.
- Treat the map as a living artifact with regular updates.

## Pitfalls
- A map created once and never updated loses its value.
- Overlapping, missing, or conflicting stories should be caught during team review.
- The article offers little further detail on common pitfalls.

## Templates and Layout
- Physical setup uses sticky notes: activities at the top, tasks beneath, stories below those, with horizontal lines for releases.
- Digital setups can use diagramming tools such as MS Visio, or collaboration boards for remote work.
- Store the final map in a versioned tool such as SharePoint or Confluence, with automatic change notifications.
